flags: Vital Farms withdrew its previously issued Fiscal 2030 financial targets.

Vital Farms lowered its fiscal 2026 outlook to net revenue of around $730 million (from $775 million to $800 million) and an Adjusted EBITDA loss of around $(15) million (from a gain between $0 and $10 million).
During 2026, Vital Farms implemented a workforce reduction impacting approximately 12% of its remote crew members and incurred 3,312 (table in thousands) of restructuring and severance costs.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 2025 10-K Item 1 (P1) and Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: Vital Farms produces shell eggs, butter, hard-boiled eggs, and liquid whole eggs, offering 29 retail stock keeping units (SKUs) through a multi-channel retail distribution network (up from 23 SKUs across more than 24,000 stores as of December 2025).
quotes: We produce products sourced from animals raised on family farms, including shell eggs, butter, hard-boiled eggs and liquid whole eggs.
As of December 2025, we offered 23 retail stock keeping units, or SKUs, through a multi-channel retail distribution network across more than 24,000 stores.
We offer 29 retail stock keeping units, or SKUs, through a multi-channel retail distribution network.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 2025 10-K Item 1A (P2) and Item 7 MD&A (P3).
business_model.claim: Shell eggs accounted for approximately 95% of net revenue in fiscal 2023 and 93% in fiscal 2024 and fiscal 2025, while eggs and egg-related products generated $733.2 million, or approximately 97%, of net revenue in fiscal 2025.
quotes: Shell eggs accounted for approximately 95% of our net revenue in fiscal 2023, 93% of our net revenue in fiscal 2024 and 93% of our net revenue in fiscal 2025.
Eggs and egg-related products generated $733.2 million, or approximately 97%, of net revenue in fiscal 2025.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: In May 2026, Vital Farms made the strategic decision to wind down its butter business by the end of fiscal 2026 to focus on its core egg product categories.
quotes: In May 2026, we made the strategic decision to wind down our butter business to sharpen our focus on our core egg product categories where we see distinct competitive advantages.
We expect to complete the wind-down of the butter business by the end of fiscal 2026.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 2025 10-K MD&A (P3) and Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: Vital Farms sells on a purchase-order basis to natural retailers, mainstream retailers, distributors, and foodservice customers, distributing products primarily through a broker-distributor-retailer network.
quotes: We generate net revenue primarily from sales of our products, including eggs and butter, to our customers, which include natural retailers, mainstream retailers, distributors and foodservice customers.
We sell our products to customers on a purchase-order basis.

Our products are primarily distributed through a broker-distributor-retailer network whereby brokers represent our products to distributors and retailers who will in turn sell our products to consumers.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 2025 10-K MD&A (P3), Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4), and Q3 2026 earnings release (P6).
business_model.claim: Vital Farms sells to retail partners including Whole Foods, Kroger, Sprouts, Target, Albertsons, Publix, and Walmart, generating retail channel net revenue of $727.9 million in fiscal 2025 ($582.4 million in fiscal 2024) and $175.1 million in the third quarter of 2026 ($189.7 million in the third quarter of 2025).
quotes: We have a strong presence at The Kroger Co., or Kroger, Sprouts Farmers Market, Target Corporation and Whole Foods Market, Inc., or Whole Foods, and we also sell our products at Albertsons Companies, Inc., Publix Super Markets, Inc., Walmart, Inc. and other retailers.
Net revenue from sales through our retail channel was $727.9 million and $582.4 million for fiscal years ended 2025 and 2024, respectively.
Net revenue from sales through our retail channel was $175.1 million and $189.7 million for the 13-week periods ended September 27, 2026 and September 28, 2025, respectively.

business_model.claim: Based on third-party data and internal analysis, Whole Foods accounted for approximately 23%, 23%, and 20% of Vital Farms' retail sales in fiscal years 2023, 2024, and 2025, respectively.
quotes: Based on this third-party data and internal analysis, Whole Foods accounted for approximately 23%, 23% and 20% of our retail sales for fiscal years 2023, 2024 and 2025, respectively.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: During periods of oversupply, Vital Farms sells or donates excess shell egg inventory to breaker and wholesale channels at reduced prices or no cost.
quotes: In periods of oversupply, we have sold or donated supply at reduced prices or no cost.
Our current oversupply of egg inventory has resulted in increased sales to breaker and wholesale channels at lower prices or no cost.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the 2025 10-K Item 1A (P2) and Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: Vital Farms sources eggs from a network of more than 600 small farms, primarily contracted family farms under buy-sell contracts in which farmers fund their own working capital, birds, and feed while Vital Farms is contractually obligated to buy all eggs produced at prices tied to pallet weight and adjusted quarterly for feed costs.
quotes: We source our eggs from a network of more than 600 small farms, including our contracted family farms along with a small number of company-owned accelerator farms.
Under these arrangements, the farmer is responsible for all of the working capital and investments required to produce the eggs and manage the farm, including purchasing the birds and feed supply.

We are contractually obligated to purchase all of the eggs produced by the farmer during the term of the contract at an agreed-upon price that depends upon pallet weight and is adjusted quarterly for changes in feed cost.
We are contractually obligated to purchase these eggs irrespective of our ability to sell such eggs.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: Collected eggs are stored at a dedicated third-party cold storage facility and washed, graded, and packed at Egg Central Station in Springfield, Missouri (capable of packing more than 7.5 million eggs per day), while plans were announced to halt construction on a second facility, Vital Crossroads in Indiana, by the end of 2026 and pause future accelerator farm development in May 2026.
quotes: Our shell eggs are collected from farmers by a third-party freight carrier.

They are then placed in cold storage at a dedicated cold storage and fulfillment center operated and owned by our longtime cold storage provider until we pack them for shipping to our customers at Egg Central Station, our state-of-the-art shell egg processing facility in Springfield, Missouri.
Egg Central Station is capable of packing more than 7.5 million eggs per day and has an SQF Excellent rating, the highest level of such certification from the Global Food Safety Initiative.

In addition, we previously announced our intention to halt construction on Vital Crossroads, our previously announced planned second egg washing and packing facility with onsite cold storage in Seymour, Indiana, by the end of 2026.
In May 2026, we also announced that we would pause the development of future accelerator farms.

business_model.claim: Fiscal 2025 net revenue rose 25% to $759,444 (table in thousands) from $606,307 (table in thousands) in fiscal 2024, driven by $78.3 million in volume growth and $74.9 million in price/mix benefits, while longer-term growth relies on expanding U.S. shell egg household penetration (approximately 10.5% versus 97.3% for the category), store count, SKU count, and retail velocity.
quotes: The increase in net revenue of $153.1 million, or 25%, was driven by volume-related increases of $78.3 million and price/mix benefits of $74.9 million.
U.S. household penetration for the shell egg category is approximately 97.3%, while the household penetration for our shell eggs is approximately 10.5%.

By capturing greater shelf space, driving higher product velocities and increasing our average SKU count per retailer, we believe there is meaningful runway for further growth with existing retail customers.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4) and Q3 2026 earnings release (P6).
business_model.claim: In 2026, economic uncertainty, industry-wide shell egg oversupply, and widened price gaps with competing shell egg products lowered retail velocities and shifted volume to breaker and wholesale channels, driving third-quarter 2026 net revenue down 8.4% year over year to $182.2 million (from $198.9 million), primarily from a $14.3 million price/mix decline and a $2.2 million non-breaker volume decline.
quotes: During 2026, as a result of economic uncertainty, an industry-wide oversupply of shell eggs and increased price gaps with certain competing shell egg products, we have experienced declining velocities in our shell egg sales to retail customers.
Net revenue decreased 8.4% to $182.2 million in the third quarter of 2026, compared to $198.9 million in the third quarter of 2025.
The decrease compared to the prior-year period was primarily driven by a price/mix decline of $14.3 million and a volume-driven decline of $2.2 million, excluding breaker and wholesale channel sales.

business_model.claim: Net revenue also varies with purchase-order timing, product and channel mix, promotional incentives (rebates, temporary price reductions, off-invoice discounts, and coupons), customer credits for non-conforming or expired products, and consumer switching when commodity shell egg prices decline relative to Vital Farms' premium pricing.
quotes: We periodically offer promotional incentives to our customers, including customer rebates, temporary price reductions, off-invoice discounts, retailer advertisements, product coupons and other trade activities.
We treat these credits and discounts as a reduction of the sales price of the related transaction at the time of sale.
As a result, low commodity shell egg prices may adversely affect our net revenue.
Net revenue may also vary from period to period depending on the purchase orders we receive, the volume and mix of our products sold, and the channels through which our products are sold.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the Q3 2026 10-Q statement of operations (F2), 2025 10-K MD&A (P3), and Q3 2026 10-Q Risk Factors (P5).
business_model.claim: Cost of goods sold — 473,762 (table in thousands), or 62% of net revenue, in fiscal 2025 and 429,268 (table in thousands) in the 9 Months Ended Sep. 27, 2026 — consists of processing labor, raw materials (eggs and butter), packaging (with shell egg cartons sourced substantially from a sole-source supplier), and overhead including utilities, insurance, inbound freight, warehouse storage, and production depreciation and amortization.
quotes: Cost of goods sold consists of the costs directly attributable to producing our products which include labor, raw material and packaging costs as well as overhead.

Overhead costs in cost of goods sold include utilities, insurance, inbound freight, storage fees related to our warehouse and depreciation and amortization expenses related to our assets used in production.
We source substantially all of our shell egg cartons from a sole source supplier, and any disruptions may impact our ability to sell our eggs.

Selling, general and administrative | 38,136 | 44,394 | 122,876 | 115,290
Shipping and distribution | $37,883 | $32,435 | $5,448 | 17%
Shipping and distribution | 11,685 | 9,169 | 33,364 | 27,004

Selling, general and administrative expenses consist primarily of broker and contractor fees for sales and marketing, as well as personnel costs for sales and marketing, finance, human resources and other administrative functions, including salaries, benefits, bonuses, stock-based compensation expense and sales commissions.
Shipping and distribution expenses consist primarily of costs related to third-party freight for our products.
The increase in shipping and distribution costs of $5.4 million, or 17%, was driven by higher sales volumes and linehaul rates.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: In 2026, costs also reflect voluntary farmer payments to curb egg supply, a workforce reduction affecting approximately 12% of remote crew members, upfront farm recruitment payments (projected at $25.0 million to $30.0 million of working capital impact in fiscal 2026), and estimated butter exit inventory write-downs of $8.0 million to $13.0 million (including $7.8 million recorded in the 39-week period ended September 27, 2026).
quotes: In the 13-week and 39-week periods ended September 27, 2026, we worked with certain of our contracted farmers to address our oversupply through voluntary amendments to their producer contracts to cease production from existing flocks or delay placement of future flocks, in return for payments to such farmers, reflecting a portion of their foregone profits.

During 2026, we have made operational staffing changes to reduce headcount and better align our resources with our growth strategies, resulting in a workforce reduction that impacted approximately 12% of our remote crew members.
We believe the impact to our working capital resulting from these upfront costs could range from $25.0 million to $30.0 million in fiscal 2026.

We estimate that the total costs incurred related to the exit of our butter business will be between $8.0 million and $13.0 million, consisting of expenses relating to inventory write-downs, inclusive of the $7.8 million in inventory obsolescence we recorded in the 39-week period ended September 27, 2026.

business_model.basis: Stated directly in the Q3 2026 10-Q MD&A (P4).
business_model.claim: Operating and supply costs are further exposed to tariffs and trade restrictions on imported equipment, packaging, and butter, inflation in materials and overhead, elevated interest rates affecting financing access, and agricultural diseases such as Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) and Egg Drop Syndrome (EDS).
quotes: Inflationary factors, such as increases in the cost of materials and supplies, interest rates and overhead costs, may adversely affect our operating results.

Elevated interest rates also present a challenge impacting the U.S. economy and could make it more difficult for us or our farmers to obtain traditional financing on acceptable terms, if at all, in the future.
We expect that tariffs and restrictions on international trade will continue to impact the cost or availability of these items.

Additionally, agricultural diseases such as HPAI or EDS have resulted and could in the future result in supply shortages and price increases across the egg market, including shortages of eggs on shelves at our retail customers.
